# Herpesviruses

> *Chickenpox in a child and shingles in the same person decades later are caused by one virus that
> never left the body, and a cold sore returns to the same spot on the lip after each fever. Every
> herpesvirus stays for life in a particular kind of cell, and that cell predicts where, and in whom,
> the virus causes disease again.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Sort the human herpesviruses by the cells in which they become latent, and predict from the
  latency site where reactivated virus causes disease and who is most at risk.
- Explain why herpes simplex viruses recur at the same site, and why shingles appears decades after
  chickenpox, over a single dermatome.
- Explain how cytomegalovirus, usually silent in a healthy person, harms a fetus and a person whose
  cell-mediated immunity is suppressed.
- Name the host, setting and route that let each main virus cause disease.
- Tell herpes simplex viruses from varicella-zoster virus by first infection, spread, recurrence and
  vaccine.
- Explain why drugs that block the herpesvirus DNA polymerase shorten an episode but cannot remove
  latent virus.
:::

## The group {#sec-herp-group}

### The group in one sentence {#sec-herp-sentence}

Herpesviruses are enveloped viruses with a double-stranded DNA genome that, after the first
infection, persist for life in a latent state in particular cells and can reactivate. Most of the six
questions have one answer for the whole group; its members differ mainly in the cells in which they
become latent.

| Question | Answer for the herpesviruses |
|---|---|
| What is it built from? | A large double-stranded DNA genome in a protein capsid, inside an envelope |
| How does it get energy? | It has no energy supply of its own and uses the host cell's |
| How does it copy itself and change? | Copies its DNA in the nucleus with its own DNA polymerase; DNA viruses change slowly, so these viruses are stable |
| Where does it live, and how does it spread? | Each human herpesvirus lives only in humans; spread by close contact with saliva, skin or genital secretions, and varicella-zoster virus also by respiratory particles; often shed without symptoms |
| How does damage happen? | Death of infected cells, in the first infection and at reactivation; damage is greatest when **cell-mediated immunity**, the defence by T cells against infected cells, is impaired |
| What does it have that my cells lack? | Its DNA polymerase, the target of the main antiviral drugs, which act only on replicating virus |

In the nucleus, the host cell's RNA polymerase transcribes herpesvirus genes as it transcribes the
cell's own, but the virus copies its genome with its own DNA polymerase (see [*How viruses are built
and copy themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-genomes)). After the first infection,
herpesviruses make new virus only when they reactivate, which places them between acute and chronic
infection on the persistence spectrum (see [*Viruses and the
host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-persistence)).

Cell-mediated immunity holds latent herpesviruses in check. When it declines with age, is suppressed
by drugs after an organ transplant, or fails as CD4 T cells are lost in advanced HIV infection (see
[*Viruses and the host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-cd4)), reactivation becomes more frequent and the
virus spreads further. The same virus therefore does more harm in a host with weaker defences (see
[*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-factors)).

The main antiviral drugs against herpesviruses block the viral DNA polymerase, so they act only on
virus whose genome is being copied (see [*Detecting viruses and antiviral
targets*](detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-targets)). They shorten an episode and, taken continuously,
can prevent disease from reactivated virus, but only while they are taken. Latent virus is a genome
that is not being copied, and the drugs cannot remove it (see [*Detecting viruses and antiviral
targets*](detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-few)).

### Sorting the group {#sec-herp-key}

Herpesviruses look alike under the electron microscope, so we sort them by the cells in which they
become latent. Three kinds of cell hold latent herpesviruses:

- Sensory nerve cells, whose cell bodies lie in a **ganglion** (plural ganglia), a cluster of nerve
  cell bodies outside the brain and spinal cord
- White blood cells of the monocyte line: monocytes, which circulate in the blood and become
  macrophages in the tissues, and the bone-marrow cells that give rise to them
- B lymphocytes, the lymphocytes that make antibodies

::: {.concept-tree}
[Sorting the herpesviruses by where they become latent]{.tree-title}

- Sensory nerve cells, in the ganglia (alphaherpesviruses)
  - Recurrences again and again at the same site: herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2
  - A widespread first illness, then, decades later, usually a single recurrence along one nerve:
    varicella-zoster virus
- White blood cells of the monocyte line (betaherpesviruses)
  - Harm to the fetus and to people with suppressed cell-mediated immunity: cytomegalovirus
  - A high fever, then a rash, in infants: human herpesvirus 6
- B lymphocytes (gammaherpesviruses)
  - Fever, sore throat and enlarged lymph nodes in adolescents; linked to some cancers:
    Epstein–Barr virus
  - A cancer of the cells lining blood and lymph vessels, in advanced HIV infection: human
    herpesvirus 8
:::

The latency site predicts where reactivated virus goes and who is most at risk:

| Where latent | What follows | Who is most at risk |
|---|---|---|
| Sensory nerve cells, in the ganglia | Reactivated virus travels back along the nerve to the skin or mucosa it supplies, so recurrences appear on a body surface, at a predictable site | Anyone who carries the virus; recurrences are more frequent and more severe when cell-mediated immunity declines |
| White blood cells of the monocyte line | These cells circulate, so reactivated virus is carried in the blood to internal organs | The fetus, and people whose cell-mediated immunity is suppressed |
| B lymphocytes | Latent virus can drive the cells it infects to keep dividing, which links these viruses to cancers | People with impaired cell-mediated immunity, in whom these cancers are more common |

Work through the key from the latency site, and read at each branch what the site predicts about the
virus.

## Main viruses {#sec-herp-main}

### Herpes simplex viruses: recurrence at the same site {#sec-herp-hsv}

Herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) and herpes simplex virus 2 (HSV-2) are two closely related viruses
with the same way of life, and about two in three people under 50 worldwide carry HSV-1
[@james2020hsv]. Like other enveloped viruses, they survive
poorly outside the body (see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-envelope)), and they spread by direct contact
with saliva, a lesion or genital secretions. Much of that spread comes from people who are shedding
virus without symptoms.

The first infection is usually in the mouth or the genital tract, where the virus multiplies in the
epithelium. It then enters the endings of the sensory nerves that supply the site and travels along
their axons to the nerve cell bodies in the ganglion, where it stays latent for life (see [*Viruses
and the host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-latency)). Either virus can infect either site, but HSV-1 is
usually latent in the trigeminal ganglion, which supplies the face, and HSV-2 in the sacral ganglia,
which supply the genital area. Fever, sunlight, stress or reduced immunity can reactivate the virus,
which travels back along the same nerve to the same site. Recurrences therefore appear in the same
place each time, as blisters on the lip (cold sores) or as genital blisters and ulcers.

HSV kills the cells it infects. Most infections cause no more than local lesions, at the first
infection and at each recurrence; three rarer patterns are serious.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| First infection at the site of entry | The virus kills epithelial cells, and fluid collects among the damaged cells as blisters, which break down into ulcers | Painful blisters and ulcers in the mouth of a young child, although many first infections cause no symptoms |
| Recurrence at the same site | Reactivated virus travels back along the sensory nerve and kills epithelial cells where the nerve ends | A cold sore at the same spot on the lip after each fever |
| Infection of the brain | The virus reaches the brain and kills nerve cells there | **Encephalitis**, inflammation of the brain: rare, but life-threatening |
| Infection of the eye | The virus infects the cornea, and repeated episodes scar it | **Keratitis**, inflammation of the cornea, which can impair sight |
| Infection during birth | Virus in the mother's genital tract infects the infant during delivery, and immature defences let it spread | Infection of a **neonate** (an infant in the first four weeks of life), which can reach the brain and other organs |

Three conditions let HSV cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | A person who carries latent virus, as most adults carry HSV-1 | The virus stays in the ganglion for life, and fever, sunlight, stress or reduced immunity reactivate it |
| Where (setting) | Close contact with saliva, a lesion or genital secretions, often from a person with no symptoms | The virus is shed without symptoms, and drying disrupts its envelope, so it passes by direct contact |
| How (route) | Through the epithelium of the mouth or genital tract, then along a sensory nerve | It infects the epithelium, travels along the axons to the ganglion and, at each reactivation, back to the same site |

Step through the two routes the herpes simplex viruses take, from a body surface to a ganglion and
back.

### Varicella-zoster virus: chickenpox, then shingles {#sec-herp-vzv}

Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) causes two illnesses, usually decades apart. It spreads by respiratory
particles and from the fluid of blisters. The first infection is **chickenpox** (varicella): the virus
multiplies in the airway, spreads in the blood (viraemia) to the skin, and causes a widespread rash of
itchy blisters. It then becomes latent in sensory ganglia, both those beside the spinal cord (the
dorsal root ganglia) and those of the cranial nerves.

Decades later, when cell-mediated immunity declines with age or with immunosuppression, the virus
reactivates in one ganglion and travels down the nerve fibres from it to the skin. The result is
**shingles** (herpes zoster), a painful band of blisters on one side of the body over a
**dermatome**, the strip of skin supplied by one spinal nerve. Pain can persist after the rash heals.
Vaccines exist against chickenpox and against shingles (see [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-prevent)).

VZV kills the cells it infects, as HSV does; the route by which it reaches the skin decides the shape
of each illness.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Widespread first infection | The virus spreads in the blood to the skin and kills epithelial cells throughout it | Chickenpox: crops of itchy blisters over the whole body |
| Reactivation along one nerve | The virus reactivates in one ganglion, damages the nerve as it travels, and kills skin cells across one dermatome | Shingles: a painful band of blisters on one side of the chest of an older adult |
| Nerve damage that outlasts the rash | Reactivation inflames and damages the sensory nerve cells and their fibres | Pain that continues for months after the rash of shingles has healed |

Three conditions let VZV cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | For chickenpox, a person who has never had chickenpox or the vaccine; for shingles, a person who had chickenpox and whose cell-mediated immunity has declined | Without immunity, the first infection spreads through the body; later, cell-mediated immunity holds the latent virus in check until it declines with age or immunosuppression |
| Where (setting) | Close contact with a person who has chickenpox or shingles | The virus is shed in respiratory particles and in the fluid of blisters |
| How (route) | Breathed in and carried in the blood to the skin; decades later, from one ganglion along one nerve | Spread in the blood gives a rash over the whole body; reactivation in a single ganglion confines shingles to one dermatome |

::: {.callout-important}
## Can shingles be caught from another person?
Shingles is often thought to be caught from someone else, partly because people with shingles are
advised to avoid close contact with those who have never had chickenpox. Shingles is reactivation of
the person's own virus, latent since chickenpox, often decades earlier, and it is not acquired from
anyone.

The fluid of shingles blisters does contain VZV, and a person who has never had chickenpox or the
vaccine can be infected by it. That person develops chickenpox, the illness of a first infection, and
not shingles.
:::

Step through the route varicella-zoster virus takes, from chickenpox to shingles decades later.

### Cytomegalovirus: harm before birth and when immunity is suppressed {#sec-herp-cmv}

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) spreads in saliva, urine, breast milk and genital secretions, and in
transplanted organs and blood. Young children shed it for long periods without symptoms. In a healthy
person the first infection usually passes unnoticed, and the virus becomes latent in white blood cells
of the monocyte line. These cells circulate, so reactivated virus is carried in the blood to organs
throughout the body.

CMV causes harm in two settings, and in both the host cannot contain it:

- A fetus can be infected across the placenta when the mother is infected during pregnancy, and the
  risk is greatest when it is her first infection. Infection passed from mother to fetus before birth
  is **congenital infection**, and congenital CMV infection is the most common non-inherited cause of
  hearing loss in childhood, present at birth or developing later [@goderis2014cmv].
- In a person whose cell-mediated immunity is suppressed, after an organ transplant or in advanced HIV
  infection, latent virus reactivates, or arrives in a donor organ, and damages the retina (the
  light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye), the lungs or the gut.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Congenital infection | Virus in the blood of a woman infected during pregnancy crosses the placenta and infects the fetus while its organs are developing | Hearing loss, present at birth or appearing in childhood |
| Reactivation when cell-mediated immunity is suppressed | Latent virus, the person's own or carried in a donor organ, reactivates; white blood cells carry it in the blood, and it kills cells in the organs it reaches | Inflammation of the gut or the lungs in the months after an organ transplant; **retinitis**, inflammation of the retina, which threatens sight in advanced HIV infection |

Three conditions let CMV cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | A fetus whose mother is infected during pregnancy; a person whose cell-mediated immunity is suppressed, after an organ transplant or in advanced HIV infection | The fetus cannot yet contain the virus; in the immunosuppressed host, the T cells that hold latent virus in check are suppressed or lost |
| Where (setting) | Close contact with young children, who shed the virus in saliva and urine; sexual contact; an organ or blood from a donor who carries the virus | Virus is shed for long periods without symptoms, and latent virus travels inside the donor's white blood cells |
| How (route) | Across the placenta; or reactivation in white blood cells, which carry the virus in the blood | Virus in the blood reaches the fetus, or the retina, the lungs and the gut |

Step through the two routes by which cytomegalovirus causes harm.

## Beyond the main viruses {#sec-herp-beyond}

### Supporting viruses {#sec-herp-supporting}

| Virus | Where it is latent | What separates it | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Epstein–Barr virus | B lymphocytes | Spread in saliva; a first infection in early childhood is usually silent, but in adolescents and young adults it often causes **infectious mononucleosis**, an illness of fever, sore throat and enlarged lymph nodes | Linked to some **lymphomas**, cancers of lymphocytes, and to **nasopharyngeal carcinoma**, a cancer of the lining of the space behind the nose that is particularly common in east and southeast Asia, including Singapore [@chen2019npc] |
| Human herpesvirus 6 | White blood cells of the monocyte line | Infects most people in early childhood | Causes **roseola**: a high fever in an infant, then a rash as the fever settles |
| Human herpesvirus 8 | B lymphocytes | Usually silent; causes disease mainly in advanced HIV infection, when cell-mediated immunity fails | Causes **Kaposi sarcoma**, a cancer of the cells lining blood and lymph vessels that forms purple patches in the skin |

### Later in the course {#sec-herp-later}

| Virus | Where it comes up again |
|---|---|
| Herpes simplex viruses | Dermatology and sexual health (cold sores and genital herpes); neurology (encephalitis); ophthalmology (keratitis); obstetrics and neonatology (neonatal herpes) |
| Varicella-zoster virus | Dermatology and paediatrics (chickenpox); neurology (shingles and the pain that can follow it); vaccines in immunology |
| Cytomegalovirus | Obstetrics and neonatology (congenital infection); transplant medicine and HIV care (reactivation); ophthalmology (retinitis) |
| Epstein–Barr virus | Haematology (infectious mononucleosis and lymphomas); head-and-neck oncology (nasopharyngeal carcinoma) |
| Human herpesvirus 6 | Paediatrics (roseola) |
| Human herpesvirus 8 | HIV care (Kaposi sarcoma) |
